questions.q: Why is high correlation between two price series not sufficient justification for a pairs trade?
options: Correlation is always zero for financial assets
Two correlated series can still drift apart permanently; only cointegration implies a stable, mean-reverting relationship between them
Correlation can only be measured for currencies
Correlation requires more data than cointegration
questions.explain: Correlation describes how two series move together over a sample, but says nothing about whether their relationship is stable long-run. Cointegration specifically tests for a mean-reverting relationship, which is what a pairs trade requires.

questions.q: What does the Engle-Granger two-step procedure actually test?
options: Whether the two raw price series have the same average value
Whether the residual from regressing one series on the other (the spread) is itself stationary
Whether the two assets are in the same sector
Whether trading volume is correlated between the two assets
questions.explain: The procedure regresses one series on the other, then tests the regression's residual — the spread — for stationarity (e.g., via an Augmented Dickey-Fuller test), which is the actual evidence for cointegration.

questions.q: In the spread formula spread = log(A) - beta * log(B), what does "long the spread" mean as a position?
options: Long A only, with no position in B
Long A and short beta units of B
Short both A and B equally
Long B and short A
questions.explain: "Long the spread" means buying A and selling beta units of B, betting the spread will rise back toward its mean. "Short the spread" is the reverse position.

questions.q: Why is "market-neutral" not the same as "risk-free" for a pairs trade?
options: Market-neutral positions still carry risks like a permanently broken cointegrating relationship, hedge-ratio estimation error, and correlated crowding across similar pairs
Market-neutral strategies are automatically profitable regardless of execution
Market-neutral only applies to bonds, not equities
There is no difference — the two terms mean the same thing
questions.explain: Removing exposure to broad market direction does not remove risks specific to the pair itself, such as the relationship breaking down, mis-estimated hedge ratios, or many firms unwinding similar trades at once.

questions.q: What historically caused sudden, sharp losses across many statistical arbitrage desks simultaneously, even though their individual pair relationships looked stable?
options: A single company's earnings miss
Crowded positioning — many desks holding economically similar pairs needed to unwind at the same time, causing correlated moves no individual pair's history would predict
A change in a stock exchange's opening hours
An increase in dividend payments
questions.explain: When many stat-arb participants hold similar pairs and need to unwind together (as happened industry-wide in August 2007), the resulting correlated selling can move spreads violently in a way the individual pair's own history never suggested.
